node_title: Add Japanese Yen (JPY) Currency Display Support
node_bodyText:
Overview
This PR adds support for displaying Claude Code usage costs in Japanese Yen (JPY) alongside the existing USD display. Users can now switch between USD and JPY with a persistent preference that is maintained across sessions.
Changes
Main Changes

Currency Conversion: Implemented JPY support with a fixed conversion rate of 1 USD = 150 JPY
Persistent Configuration: Added configuration storage using the conf library for cross-platform support
CLI Enhancement: Added --currency flag to all commands for easy currency switching
Number Formatting: Improved number formatting with comma separators for better readability

Technical Details

Modified Files:

utils.ts - Updated formatCurrency() to support multiple currencies
commands/daily.ts & commands/session.ts - Integrated currency-aware formatting
shared-args.ts - Added --currency CLI argument
README.md - Added currency feature documentation


New Files:

config.ts - Configuration management module
currency.ts - Currency conversion and formatting logic
config.test.ts & currency.test.ts - Comprehensive test coverage


Dependencies:

Added conf@13.1.0 for configuration storage
Added @types/conf@3.0.3 for TypeScript support


Configuration:

Config stored in platform-specific locations (macOS/Linux: ~/.config/ccusage/config.json, Windows: %APPDATA%\ccusage\config.json)



Impact

Breaking Changes: No - Existing functionality remains unchanged, USD is still the default
Database Changes: No
API Changes: No - JSON output format remains unchanged (always shows USD values)
Performance Impact: Negligible - Only adds configuration file read on startup

Testing

 Unit tests pass
 Integration tests pass
 Manual testing completed
 Performance testing (not applicable)

Test Details

Added 13 new tests covering currency conversion, formatting, and configuration persistence
Updated existing tests to support the new formatCurrency signature
All 47 tests pass successfully
Test coverage includes:

USD to JPY conversion accuracy
Number formatting with comma separators
Currency symbol display ($ vs ¥)
Decimal place handling (2 for USD, 0 for JPY)
Configuration persistence across sessions
Invalid currency handling



Deployment

Special Instructions: None - the feature is self-contained
Environment Variables: None required
Migration Steps: None - configuration is created automatically on first use

Review Focus Areas

Currency Conversion Rate: Currently hardcoded at 1 USD = 150 JPY - is this acceptable or should it be configurable?
Number Formatting: Using toLocaleString('en-US') for both currencies - should JPY use a different locale?
Configuration Location: Using the conf library's default paths - are these appropriate for the project?

Related Information

Issue/Ticket: Not linked to a specific issue
Documentation: README.md updated with currency configuration section
Screenshots:

Example output with JPY display:

Hello @zenmush, I'm Gemini Code Assist1! I'm currently reviewing this pull request and will post my feedback shortly. In the meantime, here's a summary to help you and other reviewers quickly get up to speed!
Summary of Changes
Hello team, gemini-code-assist here to provide a summary of this pull request from @zenmush. This PR introduces support for displaying Claude Code usage costs in Japanese Yen (JPY) in addition to the existing USD display. It adds a --currency flag to the CLI commands (daily and session) allowing users to switch between currencies. The chosen currency preference is persisted across sessions using a new configuration file. The changes involve adding new modules for currency handling and configuration, updating existing command files to use the new currency logic, and updating the README documentation.
Highlights

JPY Currency Support: Adds the ability to display usage costs in Japanese Yen (JPY) alongside the default USD.
Persistent Currency Preference: Introduces configuration management using the conf library to save the user's preferred currency across sessions.
CLI --currency Flag: Adds a new --currency flag to the daily and session commands, allowing users to specify 'USD' or 'JPY' for the output currency. Using this flag also updates the persistent preference.
Currency Conversion and Formatting: Implements logic for converting USD costs to JPY using a fixed rate (1 USD = 150 JPY) and formats the output with the correct currency symbol ($ or ¥) and decimal places (2 for USD, 0 for JPY).
Improved Number Formatting: Updates currency formatting to use locale-aware methods (toLocaleString) for better readability with comma separators.

bodyText:
Code Review
This is a well-executed PR that successfully adds JPY currency support, persistent configuration, and related CLI enhancements. The code is clearly structured, with good separation of concerns in the new config.ts and currency.ts modules. The addition of 13 new tests, covering currency conversion, formatting, and configuration persistence, is excellent and significantly boosts confidence in the changes. The README updates are also clear and helpful.
Regarding the review focus areas you raised:

Currency Conversion Rate: The hardcoded rate is simple. My comment on currency.ts (L3-6) offers thoughts on future configurability if precision becomes more critical.
Number Formatting: Using en-US locale for JPY is acceptable for consistency. My comment on currency.ts (L34) includes a note on ja-JP as an alternative for consideration.
Configuration Location: The conf library's default paths are standard and appropriate for this type of application.

Overall, great work on this feature! The code quality is high, and the new functionality is well-integrated.
Summary of Findings

Hardcoded Currency Conversion Rate: The JPY conversion rate is hardcoded (1 USD = 150 JPY). While simple, this may not reflect real-time values. This was a point of discussion raised by the author and is acceptable for the current scope but could be a future enhancement area if more precision is needed.
Number Formatting Locale for JPY: JPY amounts are formatted using the 'en-US' locale for number separation and then the '¥' symbol is prepended. This is consistent but differs from native 'ja-JP' currency formatting. This was a point of discussion raised by the author and the current approach is acceptable for consistency.
Currency Validation: The currency validation logic is present in parseCurrencyArg and setCurrency. Consider centralizing it in setCurrency for better maintainability.

Merge Readiness
The pull request is in excellent shape and implements the described features effectively. The new tests and clear code structure are commendable. The comments provided are intended for consideration rather than as blockers. I believe this PR is ready for merging. As an AI, I am not authorized to approve pull requests; please ensure it undergoes any further required human review and approval processes.

This pull request introduces significant enhancements to the cost calculation functionality, updates to the schema for usage data, and improvements to testing and debugging capabilities. The most important changes include adding support for cost calculation modes, integrating LiteLLM pricing data, expanding the schema for usage data, and refining session data handling.
Cost Calculation Enhancements:

Added three cost calculation modes (auto, calculate, display) to control how costs are computed based on token counts or pre-calculated costUSD values. ([[1]](https://github.com/ryoppippi/ccusage/pull/5/files#diff-6ebdb617a8104a7756d0cf36578ab01103dc9f07e4dc6feb751296b9c402faf7R22-R30), [[2]](https://github.com/ryoppippi/ccusage/pull/5/files#diff-b335630551682c19a781afebcf4d07bf978fb1f8ac04c6bf87428ed5106870f5R116-R120), [[3]](https://github.com/ryoppippi/ccusage/pull/5/files#diff-b335630551682c19a781afebcf4d07bf978fb1f8ac04c6bf87428ed5106870f5R141-R145), [[4]](https://github.com/ryoppippi/ccusage/pull/5/files#diff-b335630551682c19a781afebcf4d07bf978fb1f8ac04c6bf87428ed5106870f5R156-R165))
Implemented logic to calculate costs dynamically using LiteLLM pricing data when the mode is set to calculate or fallback to auto mode. ([[1]](https://github.com/ryoppippi/ccusage/pull/5/files#diff-9ef087b6a8799e1e3852522a758149979ace890a62c820a6d12a36e3eb7cc5fcR91-R93), [[2]](https://github.com/ryoppippi/ccusage/pull/5/files#diff-9ef087b6a8799e1e3852522a758149979ace890a62c820a6d12a36e3eb7cc5fcL108-R155), [[3]](https://github.com/ryoppippi/ccusage/pull/5/files#diff-9ef087b6a8799e1e3852522a758149979ace890a62c820a6d12a36e3eb7cc5fcL153-R200), [[4]](https://github.com/ryoppippi/ccusage/pull/5/files#diff-9ef087b6a8799e1e3852522a758149979ace890a62c820a6d12a36e3eb7cc5fcR238-R287))

LiteLLM Integration:

Integrated LiteLLM's pricing database to fetch model-specific pricing data for cost calculations. ([[1]](https://github.com/ryoppippi/ccusage/pull/5/files#diff-6ebdb617a8104a7756d0cf36578ab01103dc9f07e4dc6feb751296b9c402faf7R53), [[2]](https://github.com/ryoppippi/ccusage/pull/5/files#diff-9ef087b6a8799e1e3852522a758149979ace890a62c820a6d12a36e3eb7cc5fcR91-R93), [[3]](https://github.com/ryoppippi/ccusage/pull/5/files#diff-9ef087b6a8799e1e3852522a758149979ace890a62c820a6d12a36e3eb7cc5fcL108-R155))
Added validation to ensure model names in tests match LiteLLM's database entries to prevent failures caused by unsupported models. ([CLAUDE.mdR63-R86](https://github.com/ryoppippi/ccusage/pull/5/files#diff-6ebdb617a8104a7756d0cf36578ab01103dc9f07e4dc6feb751296b9c402faf7R63-R86))

Schema Updates:

Expanded the UsageDataSchema and SessionUsageSchema to include optional fields for model names and versions, enabling more detailed tracking of usage data. ([[1]](https://github.com/ryoppippi/ccusage/pull/5/files#diff-9ef087b6a8799e1e3852522a758149979ace890a62c820a6d12a36e3eb7cc5fcR7-R29), [[2]](https://github.com/ryoppippi/ccusage/pull/5/files#diff-9ef087b6a8799e1e3852522a758149979ace890a62c820a6d12a36e3eb7cc5fcR54))
Enhanced session data handling to include unique versions used within a session and sort results by last activity instead of total cost. ([[1]](https://github.com/ryoppippi/ccusage/pull/5/files#diff-9ef087b6a8799e1e3852522a758149979ace890a62c820a6d12a36e3eb7cc5fcL153-R200), [[2]](https://github.com/ryoppippi/ccusage/pull/5/files#diff-9ef087b6a8799e1e3852522a758149979ace890a62c820a6d12a36e3eb7cc5fcL215-R303))

Debugging and Testing Improvements:

Added debugging utilities (detectMismatches, printMismatchReport) to identify discrepancies in data and provide detailed reports. ([[1]](https://github.com/ryoppippi/ccusage/pull/5/files#diff-a22e1a0044d16770257ddea66c38e5d9a02b67ee541793687e483fce477e5835R11-R26), [[2]](https://github.com/ryoppippi/ccusage/pull/5/files#diff-a22e1a0044d16770257ddea66c38e5d9a02b67ee541793687e483fce477e5835R42-R47), [[3]](https://github.com/ryoppippi/ccusage/pull/5/files#diff-6f9669bd0d0825f4042a8b411bc063f5a8df5d557c7421b91ffb72c5ceb75c26R11-R26), [[4]](https://github.com/ryoppippi/ccusage/pull/5/files#diff-6f9669bd0d0825f4042a8b411bc063f5a8df5d557c7421b91ffb72c5ceb75c26R42-R47))
Updated testing guidelines to ensure comprehensive coverage for supported Claude 4 models and compatibility with LiteLLM pricing data. ([[1]](https://github.com/ryoppippi/ccusage/pull/5/files#diff-6ebdb617a8104a7756d0cf36578ab01103dc9f07e4dc6feb751296b9c402faf7R63-R86), [[2]](https://github.com/ryoppippi/ccusage/pull/5/files#diff-8154d3524d88625e7af075f901b613ca1232ec13895d54b8c0fd3c0796f1aeccR49), [[3]](https://github.com/ryoppippi/ccusage/pull/5/files#diff-8154d3524d88625e7af075f901b613ca1232ec13895d54b8c0fd3c0796f1aeccR60))

Hello @ryoppippi, I'm Gemini Code Assist1! I'm currently reviewing this pull request and will post my feedback shortly. In the meantime, here's a summary to help you and other reviewers quickly get up to speed!
Summary of Changes
As Gemini, I've reviewed this pull request which focuses on enhancing the cost calculation and debugging capabilities of the tool. The primary goals are to provide flexible cost reporting based on different calculation modes, integrate real-time model pricing data from LiteLLM, update the data schema to support more detailed usage information (like model and version), and introduce debugging utilities to identify discrepancies in cost reporting. Significant effort has also gone into improving the test suite, particularly around data loading and cost calculation accuracy.
Highlights

Cost Calculation Modes: Introduced three distinct modes (auto, calculate, display) via a new --mode CLI option to control how costs are determined: using pre-calculated costUSD, calculating from tokens using LiteLLM pricing, or a combination.
LiteLLM Pricing Integration: Integrated LiteLLM's model pricing database to enable dynamic cost calculation based on token usage when the calculate or auto modes are active. This fetches pricing data externally and caches it.
Schema Updates: The internal data schema (UsageDataSchema, SessionUsageSchema) has been updated to include optional fields for version and message.model, and costUSD is now optional, accommodating different data sources and enabling more detailed session reporting.
Session Data Improvements: Session data processing now tracks unique versions used within a session and the default sorting for session reports has been changed from total cost to last activity.
Debugging Utilities: Added new debug functionality (detectMismatches, printMismatchReport) accessible via a --debug flag to compare pre-calculated costUSD values with costs calculated from tokens using LiteLLM pricing, helping identify potential data inconsistencies.
Testing Enhancements: Refactored data loading tests to use fs-fixture for better isolation and added comprehensive tests covering the new cost calculation modes, LiteLLM integration, and schema changes, including handling of cache tokens and unknown models.

Code Review
This pull request introduces significant enhancements to cost calculation, schema updates, and debugging capabilities. The integration with LiteLLM for pricing data and the addition of cost calculation modes are valuable features. The refactoring of tests to use fs-fixture is a notable improvement for test reliability and maintainability. The new debugging utilities will also be very helpful.
Overall, the code is well-structured, and the changes are thoughtfully implemented with good test coverage and documentation updates. I've identified a couple of areas for potential improvement to enhance robustness and consistency.
Summary of Findings

CLI Argument Validation: The --mode CLI argument could benefit from explicit validation against the allowed CostModes to provide clearer feedback for invalid user input, rather than silently falling back to 'auto' mode.
Path Consistency in Debug Tooling: The detectMismatches function appears to scan a different default directory scope for JSONL files compared to the main data loading functions, which could lead to inconsistencies if not handled carefully. Aligning the path logic would improve robustness.

Merge Readiness
The PR introduces valuable features and significant improvements. The core logic appears solid and is well-tested. However, I've raised two medium severity issues concerning argument validation and path consistency in the debug tooling. It would be beneficial to address these points to further enhance the robustness and clarity of the application. As a reviewer, I am not authorized to approve pull requests. Please ensure these changes are reviewed and approved by authorized team members after addressing the feedback.

node_title: feat: add multi-currency support with live exchange rates
node_bodyText:
Summary
This PR adds comprehensive multi-currency support to ccusage, allowing users to view Claude usage costs in their preferred currency with live exchange rates.
Key Features

🌍 20 Supported Currencies: USD, EUR, GBP, JPY, CAD, AUD, CHF, CNY, INR, IDR, SGD, HKD, KRW, MXN, BRL, ZAR, SEK, NOK, DKK, PLN
📡 Live Exchange Rates: Fetches current rates from exchangerate-api.com
⚡ Smart Caching: 2-hour local cache in ~/.claude/exchange-rates.json for performance
🛡️ Graceful Fallbacks: Falls back to USD if API fails or currency unavailable
💱 Proper Formatting: Currency-specific symbols and decimal handling (e.g., IDR shows "Rp", JPY shows no decimals)
🔧 CLI Integration: New --currency/-c flag works with all existing commands

Usage Examples
# Daily report in Indonesian Rupiah
ccusage daily --currency IDR

# Session report in Euros with JSON output
ccusage session --currency EUR --json

# British Pounds with date filtering
ccusage daily --currency GBP --since 20250101
Technical Implementation
Core Components:

CurrencyService: Handles exchange rate fetching, caching, and conversion
ExchangeRate interface: Type-safe currency data structure
convertCostToCurrency(): Utility function for USD→target conversion
Enhanced CLI args with currency validation

Architecture Decisions:

Internal calculations remain in USD (maintains LiteLLM compatibility)
Currency conversion only at display time (preserves data integrity)
Local file-based caching for offline resilience
Free API with no rate limits or registration required

Error Handling:

Network failures → fallback to stale cache → fallback to USD
Missing currencies → fallback to USD with warning
Invalid cache files → start with empty cache

Files Added/Modified
New Files:

src/currency.ts - Core currency service implementation
src/currency.test.ts - Comprehensive test coverage

Modified Files:

src/types.ts - Currency types and validation schemas
src/shared-args.ts - CLI argument definition
src/calculate-cost.ts - Currency conversion utilities
src/commands/daily.ts - Multi-currency table/JSON output
src/commands/session.ts - Multi-currency table/JSON output

Testing
✅ Comprehensive test coverage for CurrencyService including:

Exchange rate fetching with API mocking
Caching behavior and TTL validation
Error handling and fallback scenarios
Currency formatting and symbol handling

✅ Manual testing verified:

CLI flag recognition and validation
Live API integration with caching
Proper formatting in both table and JSON outputs
Graceful handling of network failures

Example Output
Table Format (IDR):
┌─────────────────┬──────────────┬──────────────┬──────────────┐
│ Date            │ Total Tokens │ Cost (IDR)   │ Last Activity│
├─────────────────┼──────────────┼──────────────┼──────────────┤
│ 2025-06-06      │   82,159,177 │ Rp1097751.35 │ 2025-06-06   │
└─────────────────┴──────────────┴──────────────┴──────────────┘

JSON Format (EUR):
{
  "daily": [
    {
      "date": "2025-06-06",
      "totalCost": 59.01,
      "currency": "EUR"
    }
  ],
  "totals": {
    "totalCost": 76.77,
    "currency": "EUR"
  }
}
Backward Compatibility
✅ Fully backward compatible - defaults to USD if no currency specified
✅ No breaking changes to existing CLI interface or JSON structure
✅ Maintains data integrity - all internal calculations still in USD
Test Plan

 Verify CLI flag appears in help output
 Test currency conversion with live API
 Validate caching behavior and TTL expiration
 Confirm fallback handling for network errors
 Test all 20 supported currencies
 Verify table and JSON output formatting
 Check backward compatibility with no --currency flag
 Validate proper currency symbols and decimal handling

Implementation Notes
This feature enables international users to better understand their Claude Code usage costs in familiar currencies. The implementation prioritizes reliability with multiple fallback layers and maintains full backward compatibility.
The exchange rate API (exchangerate-api.com) is free, reliable, and doesn't require registration, making it ideal for this use case. Local caching ensures good performance and offline functionality.

The primary goal is to allow users to view their Claude usage costs in their preferred currency rather than being limited to USD. The changes integrate this new functionality into the existing daily and session commands, adding a new --currency flag and ensuring proper currency formatting in both table and JSON outputs. The implementation keeps internal calculations in USD for consistency and performs conversion only at the display layer.
Highlights

Multi-Currency Support: Adds a new --currency (or -c) CLI flag to specify the desired output currency. Supports 20 different currencies.
Live Exchange Rates: Integrates with the exchangerate-api.com service to fetch current exchange rates relative to USD.
Local Caching: Implements a local cache for exchange rates in ~/.claude/exchange-rates.json with a 2-hour TTL to improve performance and provide offline capability.
Robust Fallbacks: Includes logic to gracefully handle API failures by falling back to stale cached rates, and ultimately falling back to USD if no valid rate can be obtained.
Currency Formatting: Adds currency-specific formatting, including symbols and decimal place handling (e.g., no decimals for JPY/KRW).
CLI Integration: Modifies the daily and session commands to accept the new --currency flag and display costs in the selected currency in both table and JSON output formats.
New Currency Service: Introduces a dedicated CurrencyService class to encapsulate the logic for fetching, caching, converting, and formatting currency.

This pull request introduces a valuable monthly subcommand for reporting Claude Code usage, maintaining feature parity with the daily command. The code is well-structured, reuses existing utilities effectively, and the documentation updates are clear.

Code Review
This pull request makes a good step towards stricter validation for date and month fields by introducing regex. The changes improve format enforcement in DailyUsageSchema and MonthlyUsageSchema.
I have a couple of suggestions to further enhance the robustness of these validations, particularly concerning the actual calendar validity of dates and months, not just their string format. This will help prevent potential issues with data processing, such as sorting or filtering, if malformed (though correctly formatted) date/month strings were to enter the system.
Summary of Findings

Date field validation robustness: The DailyUsageSchema.date field validation checks for YYYY-MM-DD format but allows invalid calendar dates (e.g., 2023-02-31). This could lead to issues in sorting or date calculations. Suggested using v.isoDate() for stricter validation.

The pull request introduces useful regex-based format validation. Add Sort Order Support for Daily and Monthly Reports
Feature #11
Summary
This PR adds a new --order (-o) flag to control the sort order of dates in both daily and monthly usage reports. Users can now choose between descending (newest first, default) and ascending (oldest first) order, providing more flexibility in how they view their Claude usage data.
Motivation
Previously, both daily and monthly reports were hard-coded to display dates in descending order (newest first). While this is often the desired behavior, some users may prefer to see their usage chronologically from oldest to newest, especially when:

Tracking usage growth over time
Analyzing historical trends
Comparing early usage patterns with recent ones
Generating reports for documentation that should read chronologically

Implementation Details
Changes Made


Added --order flag to shared arguments (src/shared-args.ts)

Short flag: -o
Long flag: --order
Choices: desc (default) or asc
Consistent naming between short and long forms for intuitive CLI usage



Extended LoadOptions interface (src/data-loader.ts)

Added optional order?: "desc" | "asc" property
Maintains backward compatibility with default "desc" behavior



Updated sorting logic in data loaders

loadDailyUsageData: Sorts daily entries based on the order parameter
loadMonthlyUsageData: Sorts monthly aggregations based on the order parameter
Refactored to use fast-sort consistently and eliminate code duplication



Updated command implementations

Both daily and monthly commands now pass the order option to their respective data loaders
No changes to output format or data structure



Comprehensive test coverage

Added tests for ascending order sorting in daily reports
Added tests for ascending order sorting in monthly reports
Added tests for explicit descending order (ensuring default behavior is preserved)
Added tests for year boundary handling in monthly sorting



Documentation updates

Updated README.md with the new -o, --order flag documentation
Clear explanation of the two sort options and their effects



Code Quality Improvements
During implementation, I also addressed a code review suggestion to reduce duplication in the sorting logic:

Extracted the sort() call into a variable to avoid calling it twice in conditional branches
Applied this pattern consistently in both daily and monthly sorting functions
Switched monthly sorting to use fast-sort library for consistency

Usage Examples
# Daily reports
ccusage daily -o asc          # Show oldest days first
ccusage daily -o desc         # Show newest days first (default)
ccusage daily                 # Same as -o desc

# Monthly reports  
ccusage monthly -o asc        # Show oldest months first
ccusage monthly -o desc       # Show newest months first (default)
ccusage monthly               # Same as -o desc

# Combined with other flags
ccusage daily -o asc -j       # JSON output with ascending order
ccusage monthly -o asc -s 20240101 -u 20241231  # Filter and sort
Testing
All existing tests pass, plus new tests added:

✅ sorts by date ascending when order is 'asc' (daily)
✅ sorts by date descending when order is 'desc' (daily)
✅ sorts months in ascending order when order is 'asc' (monthly)
✅ handles year boundaries correctly in sorting (monthly)

bun test           # All 100 tests pass
bun run lint       # No lint errors
bun typecheck      # No type errors
Breaking Changes
None. The default behavior remains unchanged (descending order), ensuring backward compatibility for existing users and scripts.
Future Considerations
This implementation provides a foundation for potential future enhancements:

Sort by other criteria (e.g., cost, token count)
Multi-level sorting options
Custom sort expressions

However, these are out of scope for this PR, which focuses on the immediate need for basic chronological ordering.

Code Review
This pull request successfully refactors loadDailyUsageData, loadSessionData, and loadMonthlyUsageData to use Object.groupBy for aggregating data. This change makes the grouping intent very clear and leverages a modern JavaScript feature.
The implementation correctly handles the Partial<Record<K, T[]>> return type of Object.groupBy by checking for null or undefined entry arrays and filtering them out, which is good practice.
One notable improvement in loadSessionData is the addition of default values for sessionId and projectPath when parsing file paths, enhancing robustness.

Potential Performance Impact in loadDailyUsageData: The refactor to use Object.groupBy in loadDailyUsageData results in multiple iterations over the collected entries (grouping, then mapping/reducing, then filtering). This could be less performant than the previous single-pass Map-based aggregation for large datasets.
Potential Performance Impact in loadSessionData: In loadSessionData, after grouping by session, each session's data is iterated multiple times (to find the latest entry, to collect versions, and to sum totals). This contrasts with the previous incremental update approach and might affect performance for sessions with many entries.
Potential Performance Impact in loadMonthlyUsageData: The loadMonthlyUsageData function now performs Object.groupBy and subsequent aggregation on the results of loadDailyUsageData. This means the dailyData array is iterated multiple times after it has already been computed, potentially adding overhead.

node_title: chore: migrate from biome to eslint
node_bodyText:
I love biome because it is really fast.
However biome is missing some rules like strict-boolean-check or prefer-nullish-coalescing.
Because more and more people getting interest to ccusage(thank you guys!), I'd like to keep the linter rule more strict to avoid dangerous codes.
Also this helps AI as well.
My only concern about this is speed, but you know...
All rules are available here
https://eslint-config.ryoppippi.com/configs
bodyText:
Code Review
This pull request successfully migrates the project from Biome to ESLint for linting and formatting. The changes are comprehensive and align well with the goal of adopting stricter linting rules, as mentioned in the PR description (e.g., strict-boolean-expressions, prefer-nullish-coalescing).
Key improvements include:

Consistent code style enforced by ESLint (single quotes, import order, etc.).
Enhanced code robustness through practices like using != null for checks and ?? for nullish coalescing.
Improved type safety with explicit return types in some functions and casting JSON.parse results to unknown before validation.
A significant correctness fix by adding await to an asynchronous server start call.

The documentation and project configuration files (.gitignore, package.json, tsconfig.json, etc.) have been updated appropriately to reflect this migration. Overall, these changes enhance code quality, maintainability, and correctness. Great work on this migration!
Summary of Findings

Correctness Improvement in MCP Command: Added await to server.start() in src/commands/mcp.ts, ensuring asynchronous server startup completes before proceeding. This is a critical fix for potential race conditions.
Enhanced Code Robustness: Improved robustness by consistently using != null for checks (guards against both null and undefined) and ?? (nullish coalescing operator) for default values. This makes the code less prone to errors with unexpected falsy values.
Improved Type Safety and Clarity: Enhanced type safety by adding explicit return types to functions like createTotalsObject and by casting JSON.parse() results to unknown before validation. This improves maintainability and developer understanding.
Consistent Code Style via ESLint: The migration to ESLint (using @ryoppippi/eslint-config) has enforced a consistent code style across the project, including changes like single quotes for strings, standardized import ordering, and consistent arrow function syntax. This improves readability and maintainability.
TypeScript Definition Style: Consistently changed interface definitions to type aliases (e.g., in src/data-loader.ts, src/debug.ts, src/types.ts). This is a common stylistic preference in modern TypeScript projects, likely enforced by the new ESLint configuration. (Severity: low, not commented inline per settings)
ESLint Rule Disabling: Appropriately used eslint-disable comments for no-top-level-await in the CLI entry point (src/commands/index.ts) and for no-console in the logger utility (src/logger.ts). These are justified exceptions. (Severity: low, not commented inline per settings)

Merge Readiness
The pull request is in excellent shape. The migration to ESLint has been executed thoroughly, and the associated code changes have improved code style, robustness, and correctness. The critical fix in mcp.ts is particularly valuable. I believe these changes are ready to be merged after standard CI checks pass. As I am an AI, I am not authorized to approve pull requests; please ensure another human reviewer approves this before merging.

node_title: feat: add --fetch CLI argument for custom model pricing data sources
node_bodyText:
Summary

Implements the --fetch CLI argument requested in issue #12
Allows users to specify custom URLs or local file paths for model pricing data
Enables users behind corporate proxies to access pricing information

Changes

Added --fetch argument to shared CLI arguments with support for both HTTPS URLs and local filesystem paths
Updated PricingFetcher class to accept custom data sources in constructor
Modified all commands (daily, monthly, session) to pass the fetch parameter
Updated debug functionality to use custom pricing sources
Maintained full backward compatibility with default LiteLLM pricing

Test plan

 Build succeeds without errors
 All existing tests pass (106/106)
 Linting passes
 Manual testing with both local file and HTTPS URL works correctly
 Default behavior unchanged when --fetch is not specified
 Help text displays the new option correctly

Examples
Using a local file:
ccusage daily --fetch /path/to/pricing.json
Using a custom HTTPS URL:
ccusage daily --fetch https://example.com/custom-pricing.json
Resolves #12
🤖 Generated with Claude Code

Summary by CodeRabbit


New Features

Added a new command-line option to specify a custom source (URL or local file) for model pricing data in all commands.
Enhanced flexibility for cost calculations by allowing the use of external or local pricing databases.



Documentation

Updated documentation to explain the new option, its usage, and its effect on different calculation modes, including usage examples.

337-353: Redundant await inside hot path
calculateCostForEntry only does async work on the first call (pricing load).
Awaiting it for every record forces the loop to run sequentially and can be a bottleneck for
large JSONL files.
- cost = await calculateCostForEntry(data, mode, fetcher);
+ costPromises.push(calculateCostForEntry(data, mode, fetcher));
…
- for (const p of costPromises) { … }
Even a simple Promise.all after the inner loop roughly halves the runtime on large data
sets (~80 k lines).  Optional, but easy win.

node_title: feat: add --fetch CLI argument for custom model pricing data sources
node_bodyText:
Summary

Implements the --fetch CLI argument requested in issue #12
Allows users to specify custom URLs or local file paths for model pricing data
Enables users behind corporate proxies to access pricing information

Changes

Added --fetch argument to shared CLI arguments with support for both HTTPS URLs and local filesystem paths
Updated PricingFetcher class to accept custom data sources in constructor
Modified all commands (daily, monthly, session) to pass the fetch parameter
Updated debug functionality to use custom pricing sources
Maintained full backward compatibility with default LiteLLM pricing

Test plan

 Build succeeds without errors
 All existing tests pass (106/106)
 Linting passes
 Manual testing with both local file and HTTPS URL works correctly
 Default behavior unchanged when --fetch is not specified
 Help text displays the new option correctly

Examples
Using a local file:
ccusage daily --fetch /path/to/pricing.json
Using a custom HTTPS URL:
ccusage daily --fetch https://example.com/custom-pricing.json
Resolves #12
🤖 Generated with Claude Code

Summary by CodeRabbit


New Features

Added a new command-line option to specify a custom source (URL or local file) for model pricing data in all commands.
Enhanced flexibility for cost calculations by allowing the use of external or local pricing databases.



Documentation

Updated documentation to explain the new option, its usage, and its effect on different calculation modes, including usage examples.

bodyText:
Summary of Changes
Hello @constantins2001, I'm Gemini Code Assist1! I'm currently reviewing this pull request and will post my feedback shortly. In the meantime, here's a summary to help you and other reviewers quickly get up to speed!
This pull request significantly enhances the usage reporting capabilities of the tool by introducing model-specific breakdowns. Users can now see not just total usage and cost per day, month, or session, but also how that usage and cost is distributed among the different models employed, providing much finer-grained insights.
Highlights

Enhanced Usage Reports: The daily, monthly, and session usage reports now include a 'Models' column showing which models were used, and nested rows providing a breakdown of token usage and cost per model for each entry.
Data Structure Updates: Added modelsUsed (array of strings) and modelBreakdowns (array of objects detailing usage/cost per model) fields to the daily, monthly, and session usage data structures.
Data Aggregation Logic: Modified the data loading functions (loadDailyUsageData, loadSessionData, loadMonthlyUsageData) to parse model information from usage entries, aggregate tokens and cost by model, and include this breakdown data in the final report objects.
CLI Output Formatting: Updated the CLI commands (daily, monthly, session) to display the new 'Models' column and render the model breakdown data as indented, grayed-out rows beneath the main entry in the table output.


Using Gemini Code Assist

The full guide for Gemini Code Assist can be found on our documentation page, here are some quick tips.
Invoking Gemini
You can request assistance from Gemini at any point in your pull request via creating an issue comment (i.e. comment on the pull request page) using either /gemini <command> or @gemini-code-assist <command>. Below is a summary of the supported commands.



Feature

Code Review

Performs a code review for the current pull request in its current state.


Pull Request Summary
/gemini summary
Provides a summary of the current pull request in its current state.


Comment
@gemini-code-assist
Responds in comments when explicitly tagged, both in issue comments and review comments.


Help
/gemini help
Displays a list of available commands.



Customization
To customize Gemini Code Assist for GitHub experience, repository maintainers can create a configuration file and/or provide a custom code review style guide (such as PEP-8 for Python) by creating and adding files to a .gemini/ folder in the base of the repository. Detailed instructions can be found here.
Limitations & Feedback
Gemini Code Assist is currently in preview and may make mistakes. Please leave feedback on any instances where its feedback is incorrect or counter productive. You can react with 👍 and 👎 on @gemini-code-assist comments to provide feedback.
You can also get AI-powered code generation, chat, as well as code reviews directly in the IDE at no cost with the Gemini Code Assist IDE Extension.

Hello @EphemeralSapient, I'm Gemini Code Assist1! I'm currently reviewing this pull request and will post my feedback shortly. In the meantime, here's a summary to help you and other reviewers quickly get up to speed!
This pull request adds a significant new feature to the ccusage tool: the ability to analyze usage data specifically tailored to the Claude Max plan's 5-hour session window structure and its 50-session monthly limit. It provides detailed breakdowns per window and aggregates monthly statistics, including utilization and remaining sessions, to help users monitor their usage against the plan's constraints.
Highlights

New Command: Introduced a new sessions command to the CLI for tracking Claude Max plan 5-hour session windows.
Session Window Tracking: Implemented logic to group usage data entries into 5-hour windows based on the timestamp of the first message within that window's time slot.
Monthly Limit Monitoring: Added reporting for the 50-session monthly limit, showing total sessions used, remaining sessions, and utilization percentage per month.
Detailed Window Breakdown: The report includes a table detailing each 5-hour window with metrics like duration, message count, conversation count, token usage (input, output, cache), and cost.
Reporting Options: The new command supports existing options like --since, --until for date filtering, --json for machine-readable output, --mode for cost calculation, and --order for sorting monthly results.

This pull request adds a new sessions command to report Claude Code usage based on 5-hour session windows, including tracking against a monthly limit. The changes are well-tested and cover README updates, command implementation, data loading logic, and type definitions.
Key feedback points include ensuring consistency in default sort order documentation and implementation, correcting a token aggregation bug in loadSessionWindowData for monthly stats, and suggesting improvements for maintainability. The overall structure is good, and addressing these points will enhance the feature's robustness and clarity.

bodyText:
Pull Request Overview
This PR implements 5-hour session window tracking for the Claude Max plan, grouping usage into fixed windows and enforcing a 50-session monthly limit.

Defined new Zod‐style schemas (SessionWindow, CurrentSessionInfo, SessionWindowStats) in types.internal.ts
Added loadSessionWindowData, window‐grouping utilities, and current session calculation in data-loader.ts
Introduced ccusage sessions command, corresponding tests, and documentation in commands/ and README.md

Reviewed Changes
Copilot reviewed 7 out of 7 changed files in this pull request and generated 2 comments.

New CLI command for session window reports

Updated docs and usage examples for session windows report

765-768: ⚠️ Potential issue
Include all token types in monthly total tokens calculation.
The totalTokens calculation currently only sums inputTokens and outputTokens, but cache tokens (cacheCreationTokens and cacheReadTokens) are tracked separately in windows. For consistency with how tokens are aggregated elsewhere in the codebase, include all token types.
 const totals = windows.reduce((acc, window) => ({
 	cost: acc.cost + window.totalCost,
-	tokens: acc.tokens + window.inputTokens + window.outputTokens,
+	tokens: acc.tokens + window.inputTokens + window.outputTokens + window.cacheCreationTokens + window.cacheReadTokens,
 }), { cost: 0, tokens: 0 });

node_title: fix: implement chronological deduplication for branched conversations
node_bodyText:
Fix: Implement Chronological Deduplication for Branched Conversations
Summary
This PR fixes issue #19 by implementing a chronologically-aware deduplication system that prevents double-counting of tokens and costs when conversations are branched in Claude Code.
Fixes #19
Problem
When users branch conversations in Claude Code (by editing a past message with Esc+Esc), the application creates a new conversation that includes duplicate entries from the original conversation. These duplicates have identical requestId and message.id values, causing:

Inflated token counts - The same API calls are counted multiple times
Incorrect cost calculations - Users see higher costs than actually incurred
Wrong date attribution - Costs may be attributed to the branch date instead of the original date

Root Cause
The current implementation processes JSONL files in an undefined order (filesystem-dependent). This means:

A newer branched conversation file might be processed before the original
Without deduplication, both files contribute to the totals
Even with simple deduplication, processing order matters - the first processed entry "wins"

Solution
This PR implements a comprehensive deduplication solution that:
1. Chronological File Processing

Added getEarliestTimestamp() to extract the earliest timestamp from each JSONL file
Added sortFilesByTimestamp() to sort files by their earliest timestamp
Files are now processed oldest-first, ensuring original entries are preserved

2. Message Deduplication

Extended UsageDataSchema to include message.id and requestId fields
Added createUniqueHash() to generate unique identifiers from message+request IDs
Track processed hashes in a Set to skip duplicate entries
Implemented in both loadDailyUsageData() and loadSessionData()

3. Robust Implementation

Handles files without timestamps (placed at end of processing order)
Skips invalid JSON lines gracefully
Maintains backward compatibility with existing data

Testing
Added comprehensive test suite (data-loader-deduplication.test.ts) with 11 tests covering:

✅ Hash creation from message and request IDs
✅ Timestamp extraction from JSONL files
✅ File sorting by timestamp
✅ Deduplication in daily usage data
✅ Deduplication in session data
✅ Edge cases (missing IDs, invalid JSON, no timestamps)

All existing tests (117 total) continue to pass.
Code Changes
Modified Files:

src/data-loader.ts - Added deduplication logic and chronological processing
src/data-loader-deduplication.test.ts - New comprehensive test suite

Key Functions Added:
// Create unique identifier for deduplication
createUniqueHash(data: UsageData): string | null

// Extract earliest timestamp from JSONL file
getEarliestTimestamp(filePath: string): Promise<Date | null>

// Sort files chronologically
sortFilesByTimestamp(files: string[]): Promise<string[]>
Impact

Accurate Costs: Users will see correct token counts and costs
Proper Attribution: Usage is attributed to the original date, not branch date
No Data Loss: Only true duplicates are removed
Performance: Minimal overhead from sorting files before processing

Verification
Before this fix:

Branched conversations would show inflated costs
Same usage could appear on multiple dates

After this fix:

Each unique API call is counted exactly once
Usage appears only on the original date
Branched conversations no longer inflate costs

Breaking Changes
None. This change is backward compatible and transparent to users.
Future Considerations
This implementation uses a simple concatenation for the hash (messageId:requestId). If needed, this could be upgraded to use a proper hashing algorithm, though the current approach is sufficient for the use case.

Summary by CodeRabbit

New Features

Improved data loading by processing usage data files in chronological order.
Added deduplication to ensure duplicate messages are filtered out during data loading.


Bug Fixes

Prevented duplicate entries from affecting usage and session statistics.


Tests

Added comprehensive tests to verify deduplication and chronological processing of data files.

Added comprehensive test suite (data-loader-deduplication.test.ts) with 11 tests covering:

✅ Hash creation from message and request IDs
✅ Timestamp extraction from JSONL files
✅ File sorting by timestamp
✅ Deduplication in daily usage data
✅ Deduplication in session data
✅ Edge cases (missing IDs, invalid JSON, no timestamps)

All existing tests (117 total) continue to pass.
Code Changes
Modified Files:

src/data-loader.ts - Added deduplication logic and chronological processing
src/data-loader-deduplication.test.ts - New comprehensive test suite

Key Functions Added:
// Create unique identifier for deduplication
createUniqueHash(data: UsageData): string | null

// Extract earliest timestamp from JSONL file
getEarliestTimestamp(filePath: string): Promise<Date | null>

// Sort files chronologically
sortFilesByTimestamp(files: string[]): Promise<string[]>
Impact

Accurate Costs: Users will see correct token counts and costs
Proper Attribution: Usage is attributed to the original date, not branch date
No Data Loss: Only true duplicates are removed
Performance: Minimal overhead from sorting files before processing

Verification
Before this fix:

Branched conversations would show inflated costs
Same usage could appear on multiple dates

After this fix:

Each unique API call is counted exactly once
Usage appears only on the original date
Branched conversations no longer inflate costs

Breaking Changes
None. This change is backward compatible and transparent to users.
Future Considerations
This implementation uses a simple concatenation for the hash (messageId:requestId). If needed, this could be upgraded to use a proper hashing algorithm, though the current approach is sufficient for the use case.

Summary by CodeRabbit

New Features

Improved data loading by processing usage data files in chronological order.
Added deduplication to ensure duplicate messages are filtered out during data loading.


Bug Fixes

Prevented duplicate entries from affecting usage and session statistics.


Tests

Added comprehensive tests to verify deduplication and chronological processing of data files.

src/data-loader.ts (2)
108-118: Consider using a proper hashing algorithm for more robust deduplication.
The current implementation using simple concatenation works but could have edge cases if IDs contain colons. As mentioned in the PR objectives, using a proper hashing algorithm would be more robust.
+import { createHash } from 'node:crypto';

export function createUniqueHash(data: UsageData): string | null {
	const messageId = data.message.id;
	const requestId = data.requestId;

	if (messageId == null || requestId == null) {
		return null;
	}

-	// Create a hash using simple concatenation
-	return `${messageId}:${requestId}`;
+	// Create a hash using SHA-256 for collision resistance
+	return createHash('sha256')
+		.update(`${messageId}:${requestId}`)
+		.digest('hex');
}

node_bodyText:
Fix: Implement Chronological Deduplication for Branched Conversations
Summary
This PR fixes issue #19 by implementing a chronologically-aware deduplication system that prevents double-counting of tokens and costs when conversations are branched in Claude Code.
Fixes #19
Problem
When users branch conversations in Claude Code (by editing a past message with Esc+Esc), the application creates a new conversation that includes duplicate entries from the original conversation. These duplicates have identical requestId and message.id values, causing:

Inflated token counts - The same API calls are counted multiple times
Incorrect cost calculations - Users see higher costs than actually incurred
Wrong date attribution - Costs may be attributed to the branch date instead of the original date

Root Cause
The current implementation processes JSONL files in an undefined order (filesystem-dependent). This means:

A newer branched conversation file might be processed before the original
Without deduplication, both files contribute to the totals
Even with simple deduplication, processing order matters - the first processed entry "wins"

Solution
This PR implements a comprehensive deduplication solution that:
1. Chronological File Processing

Added getEarliestTimestamp() to extract the earliest timestamp from each JSONL file
Added sortFilesByTimestamp() to sort files by their earliest timestamp
Files are now processed oldest-first, ensuring original entries are preserved

2. Message Deduplication

Extended UsageDataSchema to include message.id and requestId fields
Added createUniqueHash() to generate unique identifiers from message+request IDs
Track processed hashes in a Set to skip duplicate entries
Implemented in both loadDailyUsageData() and loadSessionData()

3. Robust Implementation

Handles files without timestamps (placed at end of processing order)
Skips invalid JSON lines gracefully
Maintains backward compatibility with existing data

Testing
Added comprehensive test suite (data-loader-deduplication.test.ts) with 11 tests covering:

✅ Hash creation from message and request IDs
✅ Timestamp extraction from JSONL files
✅ File sorting by timestamp
✅ Deduplication in daily usage data
✅ Deduplication in session data
✅ Edge cases (missing IDs, invalid JSON, no timestamps)

All existing tests (117 total) continue to pass.
Code Changes
Modified Files:

src/data-loader.ts - Added deduplication logic and chronological processing
src/data-loader-deduplication.test.ts - New comprehensive test suite

Key Functions Added:
// Create unique identifier for deduplication
createUniqueHash(data: UsageData): string | null

// Extract earliest timestamp from JSONL file
getEarliestTimestamp(filePath: string): Promise<Date | null>

// Sort files chronologically
sortFilesByTimestamp(files: string[]): Promise<string[]>
Impact

Accurate Costs: Users will see correct token counts and costs
Proper Attribution: Usage is attributed to the original date, not branch date
No Data Loss: Only true duplicates are removed
Performance: Minimal overhead from sorting files before processing

Verification
Before this fix:

Branched conversations would show inflated costs
Same usage could appear on multiple dates

After this fix:

Each unique API call is counted exactly once
Usage appears only on the original date
Branched conversations no longer inflate costs

Breaking Changes
None. This change is backward compatible and transparent to users.
Future Considerations
This implementation uses a simple concatenation for the hash (messageId:requestId). If needed, this could be upgraded to use a proper hashing algorithm, though the current approach is sufficient for the use case.

Summary by CodeRabbit

New Features

Improved data loading by processing usage data files in chronological order.
Added deduplication to ensure duplicate messages are filtered out during data loading.


Bug Fixes

Prevented duplicate entries from affecting usage and session statistics.


Tests

Added comprehensive tests to verify deduplication and chronological processing of data files.

Each unique API call is counted exactly once
Usage appears only on the original date
Branched conversations no longer inflate costs

Breaking Changes
None. This change is backward compatible and transparent to users.
Future Considerations
This implementation uses a simple concatenation for the hash (messageId:requestId). If needed, this could be upgraded to use a proper hashing algorithm, though the current approach is sufficient for the use case.

Summary by CodeRabbit

New Features

Improved data loading by processing usage data files in chronological order.
Added deduplication to ensure duplicate messages are filtered out during data loading.


Bug Fixes

Prevented duplicate entries from affecting usage and session statistics.


Tests

Added comprehensive tests to verify deduplication and chronological processing of data files.

node_bodyText:
Fix: Implement Chronological Deduplication for Branched Conversations
Summary
This PR fixes issue #19 by implementing a chronologically-aware deduplication system that prevents double-counting of tokens and costs when conversations are branched in Claude Code.
Fixes #19
Problem
When users branch conversations in Claude Code (by editing a past message with Esc+Esc), the application creates a new conversation that includes duplicate entries from the original conversation. These duplicates have identical requestId and message.id values, causing:

Inflated token counts - The same API calls are counted multiple times
Incorrect cost calculations - Users see higher costs than actually incurred
Wrong date attribution - Costs may be attributed to the branch date instead of the original date

Root Cause
The current implementation processes JSONL files in an undefined order (filesystem-dependent). This means:

A newer branched conversation file might be processed before the original
Without deduplication, both files contribute to the totals
Even with simple deduplication, processing order matters - the first processed entry "wins"

Solution
This PR implements a comprehensive deduplication solution that:
1. Chronological File Processing

Added getEarliestTimestamp() to extract the earliest timestamp from each JSONL file
Added sortFilesByTimestamp() to sort files by their earliest timestamp
Files are now processed oldest-first, ensuring original entries are preserved

2. Message Deduplication

Extended UsageDataSchema to include message.id and requestId fields
Added createUniqueHash() to generate unique identifiers from message+request IDs
Track processed hashes in a Set to skip duplicate entries
Implemented in both loadDailyUsageData() and loadSessionData()

3. Robust Implementation

Handles files without timestamps (placed at end of processing order)
Skips invalid JSON lines gracefully
Maintains backward compatibility with existing data

Testing
Added comprehensive test suite (data-loader-deduplication.test.ts) with 11 tests covering:

✅ Hash creation from message and request IDs
✅ Timestamp extraction from JSONL files
✅ File sorting by timestamp
✅ Deduplication in daily usage data
✅ Deduplication in session data
✅ Edge cases (missing IDs, invalid JSON, no timestamps)

All existing tests (117 total) continue to pass.
Code Changes
Modified Files:

src/data-loader.ts - Added deduplication logic and chronological processing
src/data-loader-deduplication.test.ts - New comprehensive test suite

Key Functions Added:
// Create unique identifier for deduplication
createUniqueHash(data: UsageData): string | null

// Extract earliest timestamp from JSONL file
getEarliestTimestamp(filePath: string): Promise<Date | null>

// Sort files chronologically
sortFilesByTimestamp(files: string[]): Promise<string[]>
Impact

Accurate Costs: Users will see correct token counts and costs
Proper Attribution: Usage is attributed to the original date, not branch date
No Data Loss: Only true duplicates are removed
Performance: Minimal overhead from sorting files before processing

Verification
Before this fix:

Branched conversations would show inflated costs
Same usage could appear on multiple dates

After this fix:

Each unique API call is counted exactly once
Usage appears only on the original date
Branched conversations no longer inflate costs

Breaking Changes
None. This change is backward compatible and transparent to users.
Future Considerations
This implementation uses a simple concatenation for the hash (messageId:requestId). If needed, this could be upgraded to use a proper hashing algorithm, though the current approach is sufficient for the use case.

Summary by CodeRabbit

New Features

Improved data loading by processing usage data files in chronological order.
Added deduplication to ensure duplicate messages are filtered out during data loading.


Bug Fixes

Prevented duplicate entries from affecting usage and session statistics.


Tests

Added comprehensive tests to verify deduplication and chronological processing of data files.

node_title: fix: implement chronological deduplication for branched conversations
node_bodyText:
Fix: Implement Chronological Deduplication for Branched Conversations
Summary
This PR fixes issue #19 by implementing a chronologically-aware deduplication system that prevents double-counting of tokens and costs when conversations are branched in Claude Code.
Fixes #19
Problem
When users branch conversations in Claude Code (by editing a past message with Esc+Esc), the application creates a new conversation that includes duplicate entries from the original conversation. These duplicates have identical requestId and message.id values, causing:

Inflated token counts - The same API calls are counted multiple times
Incorrect cost calculations - Users see higher costs than actually incurred
Wrong date attribution - Costs may be attributed to the branch date instead of the original date

Root Cause
The current implementation processes JSONL files in an undefined order (filesystem-dependent). This means:

A newer branched conversation file might be processed before the original
Without deduplication, both files contribute to the totals
Even with simple deduplication, processing order matters - the first processed entry "wins"

Solution
This PR implements a comprehensive deduplication solution that:
1. Chronological File Processing

Added getEarliestTimestamp() to extract the earliest timestamp from each JSONL file
Added sortFilesByTimestamp() to sort files by their earliest timestamp
Files are now processed oldest-first, ensuring original entries are preserved

2. Message Deduplication

Extended UsageDataSchema to include message.id and requestId fields
Added createUniqueHash() to generate unique identifiers from message+request IDs
Track processed hashes in a Set to skip duplicate entries
Implemented in both loadDailyUsageData() and loadSessionData()

3. Robust Implementation

Handles files without timestamps (placed at end of processing order)
Skips invalid JSON lines gracefully
Maintains backward compatibility with existing data

Testing
Added comprehensive test suite (data-loader-deduplication.test.ts) with 11 tests covering:

✅ Hash creation from message and request IDs
✅ Timestamp extraction from JSONL files
✅ File sorting by timestamp
✅ Deduplication in daily usage data
✅ Deduplication in session data
✅ Edge cases (missing IDs, invalid JSON, no timestamps)

All existing tests (117 total) continue to pass.
Code Changes
Modified Files:

src/data-loader.ts - Added deduplication logic and chronological processing
src/data-loader-deduplication.test.ts - New comprehensive test suite

Key Functions Added:
// Create unique identifier for deduplication
createUniqueHash(data: UsageData): string | null

// Extract earliest timestamp from JSONL file
getEarliestTimestamp(filePath: string): Promise<Date | null>

// Sort files chronologically
sortFilesByTimestamp(files: string[]): Promise<string[]>
Impact

Accurate Costs: Users will see correct token counts and costs
Proper Attribution: Usage is attributed to the original date, not branch date
No Data Loss: Only true duplicates are removed
Performance: Minimal overhead from sorting files before processing

Verification
Before this fix:

Branched conversations would show inflated costs
Same usage could appear on multiple dates

After this fix:

Each unique API call is counted exactly once
Usage appears only on the original date
Branched conversations no longer inflate costs

Breaking Changes
None. This change is backward compatible and transparent to users.
Future Considerations
This implementation uses a simple concatenation for the hash (messageId:requestId). If needed, this could be upgraded to use a proper hashing algorithm, though the current approach is sufficient for the use case.

Summary by CodeRabbit

New Features

Improved data loading by processing usage data files in chronological order.
Added deduplication to ensure duplicate messages are filtered out during data loading.


Bug Fixes

Prevented duplicate entries from affecting usage and session statistics.


Tests

Added comprehensive tests to verify deduplication and chronological processing of data files.

Overall, the changes effectively address the goal of adding proxy support and fixing issues with compiled binaries.

🧹 Nitpick comments (3)

src/data-aggregation.ts (2)
32-46: Avoid repeated object-literal allocation & tighten typing
Inside the hot loop you allocate a fresh “zero” TokenStats object every time the model key is first seen.
Hoist this constant (or a factory) outside the loop, and/or use ??= to keep the existing object to avoid the extra allocation on every first encounter.
Additionally, usage is currently inferred as any, which triggers all the ts/no-unsafe- warnings reported by ESLint.  Constrain the generic to something that contains a strongly-typed usage property to silence those warnings.
-const existing = modelAggregates.get(modelName) ?? {
-  inputTokens: 0,
-  ...
-};
+const defaultStats: TokenStats = {
+  inputTokens: 0,
+  outputTokens: 0,
+  cacheCreationTokens: 0,
+  cacheReadTokens: 0,
+  cost: 0,
+};
+const existing = modelAggregates.get(modelName) ?? defaultStats;
If you introduce a generic constraint:
export function aggregateByModel<T extends { /* whatever shape */ }>(...)
you’ll eliminate the unsafe-member-access noise.

replace(/-/g, '') assumes the date string has only hyphens.
If getDate ever returns an ISO timestamp (2025-06-18T12:34:56Z) the compare logic silently breaks.
Consider normalising with new Date() and comparing epoch numbers, or slice the first 10 chars before stripping dashes:
-const dateStr = getDate(item).replace(/-/g, '');
+const dateStr = getDate(item).substring(0, 10).replace(/-/g, '');
This keeps the function tolerant to full ISO strings while preserving the cheap lexicographic compare trick.

In loadSessionData you’ve kept the old in-place deduplication (451-460) instead of using the new helpers, unlike the daily path above.

-const uniqueHash = createUniqueHash(data);
-if (uniqueHash != null && processedHashes.has(uniqueHash)) …

+const uniqueHash = createUniqueHash(data);

Summary

Remove -p short option: Removed the `-p` short option since Claude data directory can now be configured via `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` environment variable
Remove --path option entirely: Completely removed the `--path` CLI option to simplify the interface and encourage environment variable usage
Update all commands: Modified daily, monthly, session, and mcp commands to use `getDefaultClaudePath()` directly
Update documentation: Updated README to remove all references to `--path` option and clarify environment variable usage

Changes Made
CLI Interface Changes

Removed `path` argument from `shared-args.internal.ts`
Updated all command files to import and use `getDefaultClaudePath()` directly
No longer accepts `--path` or `-p` options - users must use `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` environment variable

Documentation Updates

Removed `--path` option from CLI options documentation in README
Updated usage examples to remove `--path` references
Clarified that only `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` environment variable is supported for custom paths

Test Coverage

All existing tests continue to pass
No test changes needed as the functionality remains the same, just configured differently

Breaking Change Notice
⚠️ This is a breaking change: The `--path` and `-p` options are no longer available. Users who were using these options should set the `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` environment variable instead:
```bash
Before (no longer works):
ccusage daily --path /custom/path
After:
export CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR="/custom/path"
ccusage daily
```
Test Plan

 All existing tests pass
 Linting passes
 CLI works with default path (~/.claude)
 CLI works with CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR environment variable

 Documentation updated to reflect changes

If the variable is set to a relative path ("./.claude"), contains ~, or mixes slashes, callers will receive it unchanged, which can later surface as subtle “file not found” errors when code that expects an absolute, normalised path tries to join/resolve again.
A minimal improvement is to run the env value through path.resolve (or at least path.normalize) before returning:
-	return (envPath != null && envPath.trim() !== '') ? envPath : path.join(homedir(), '.claude');
+	if (envPath != null && envPath.trim() !== '') {
+		return path.resolve(envPath.trim());
+	}
+	return path.join(homedir(), '.claude');
Keeps backward compatibility while guarding against surprising relative inputs.

ccusage daily --path /custom/path
After:
export CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR="/custom/path"
ccusage daily

src/pricing-fetcher.ts (1)
98-106: Missing new Claude-4 naming variant leads to false negatives
getModelPricing()’s heuristic list does not include the new claude-4-* naming that the tests (and likely users) now pass in:
`claude-4-${modelName}`,
Without it, look-ups such as "claude-sonnet-4-20250514" → "claude-4-sonnet-20250514" will fail.
Either extend the variations array or normalise both strings before comparison. Quick patch:
   const variations = [
     modelName,
     `anthropic/${modelName}`,
     `claude-3-5-${modelName}`,
     `claude-3-${modelName}`,
+    `claude-4-${modelName}`,

 const sessionCommand = define<{

Summary
This PR adds comprehensive offline mode support to enable cost calculations without network connectivity to the LiteLLM API. The implementation uses a build-time macro system to pre-fetch and embed pricing data directly into the binary.
Key Features

Build-time Pricing Cache: Automatically fetches and caches all Claude model pricing data during build
Offline CLI Flag: Adds --offline flag support to all commands (daily, monthly, session)
Graceful Degradation: Falls back to offline mode when network is unavailable
Full Test Coverage: Comprehensive tests for both online and offline modes

Technical Implementation

Macro System: Uses unplugin-macro to fetch LiteLLM pricing data at build time
Dual Mode Support: PricingFetcher supports both online (API) and offline (cached) modes
Consistent Interface: No changes to existing CLI usage patterns
Error Handling: Robust fallback behavior when offline data is unavailable

Usage
# Use offline mode (no network required)
ccusage daily --offline
ccusage monthly --offline
ccusage session --offline

# Online mode (default, requires network)
ccusage daily
ccusage monthly
ccusage session
Test Coverage

Online/offline mode consistency validation
Pre-fetched pricing data verification
End-to-end CLI integration tests
Error handling for edge cases

This change maintains full backward compatibility while adding the flexibility to work without network connectivity.

Summary by CodeRabbit


New Features

Added an offline mode option to the CLI, allowing users to use cached data instead of fetching from the API.
Offline mode is now available for daily, monthly, and session usage commands.
Pricing data for Claude models can now be prefetched and used in offline mode.



Bug Fixes

Updated model naming conventions in cost calculation and pricing retrieval tests.



Tests

Added tests to verify offline mode functionality and ensure cost calculation works when using cached data.



Chores

Introduced new dependencies and updated build configuration for macro support.

node_bodyText:
Summary
This PR implements a new blocks command to analyze Claude Code usage in 5-hour billing windows as requested in #23.
Features

5-Hour Block Tracking: Groups usage into Claude's 5-hour session windows that start with first message
Active Block Monitoring: Shows time elapsed/remaining and burn rate for current sessions
Token Limit Support: Set limits with -t <number> or use -t max to automatically use highest previous block
Usage Projections: Projects total usage if current burn rate continues for the full 5 hours
Recent Filter: --recent flag shows only last 3 days of blocks
Detailed Active View: --active flag shows detailed view of current active block

Implementation Details

Core logic in src/utils/five-hour-blocks.ts handles block detection and calculations
New CLI command in src/commands/blocks.ts with table and JSON output formats
Integrated with existing data loader infrastructure
Added comprehensive documentation to README

bodyText:
Actionable comments posted: 2

🧹 Nitpick comments (9)

src/utils/five-hour-blocks.ts (2)
185-188: Avoid early rounding – it degrades projection accuracy
calculateBurnRate rounds both tokensPerMinute and costPerHour, then projectBlockUsage multiplies these rounded numbers to estimate totals. On long remaining windows this can introduce noticeable drift.
Return full-precision numbers from calculateBurnRate and only round when formatting for display:
-  tokensPerMinute: Math.round(tokensPerMinute),
-  costPerHour: Math.round(costPerHour * 100) / 100,
+  tokensPerMinute,
+  costPerHour,
Then apply rounding in the CLI where the values are rendered.
Also applies to: 202-207

176-180: Zero-minute blocks produce null; consider minimum window guard
For blocks where the first and last entry share the same minute, durationMinutes becomes 0, so burn-rate is null.
If that’s unintended, clamp to at least one minute to avoid silent loss of data:
const durationMinutes = Math.max(1,
  (lastEntry.getTime() - firstEntry.getTime()) / 60000);


src/data-loader.ts (2)
843-849: Stream JSONL files instead of loading them wholesale
readFile(..., 'utf-8') followed by .split('\n') loads the entire file into memory.
Large project histories can easily reach hundreds of MB, causing high RAM spikes.
Consider using an async line iterator (createInterface from readline/promises or Bun/Deno equivalents) so lines are processed incrementally:
const rl = createInterface({ input: createReadStream(file) });
for await (const line of rl) { /* parse */ }

869-872: Cost calculation throttles I/O
await calculateCostForEntry is executed inside the tight inner loop, forcing strictly sequential processing. If PricingFetcher involves I/O (e.g. remote price fetch), total load time grows linearly with message count.
Batch-fetch prices for distinct models once, or make calculateCostForEntry synchronous by pre-seeding a local pricing table.


src/commands/blocks.ts (2)
230-260: Factor out token-limit parsing to keep CLI logic DRY
parseInt/max handling is repeated in two separate branches. A tiny helper improves readability and prevents divergent behaviour on future edits.
function resolveTokenLimit(raw: string | undefined, maxFromHistory: number): number | undefined {
  if (!raw) return undefined;
  if (raw === 'max') return maxFromHistory || undefined;
  const n = Number.parseInt(raw, 10);
  return Number.isFinite(n) ? n : undefined;
}
Then call const limit = resolveTokenLimit(ctx.values.tokenLimit, maxTokensFromAll);
Also applies to: 269-279

282-299: Header alignment relies on parallel arrays – fragile for future edits
tableHeaders and tableAligns must stay in sync manually. A small slip adds a hard-to-notice column mismatch.
Wrap these in a single array of objects { title, align } to keep structure cohesive and avoid off-by-one errors.


README.md (3)
219-223: Align section title and description with established report naming.
The heading should follow the singular "Report" convention (e.g., "5-Hour Block Report") and drop the unnecessary possessive "Claude's" in the description for consistency with other sections.

224-233: Avoid contractions in code example comments.
Replace "you'll" with "you will" in the "# Set a token limit to see if you'll exceed it" line to maintain a professional, consistent tone across examples.

255-260: Use consistent terminology for report items.
The bullet list mixes "sessions" and "blocks" (e.g., "highest previous session")—it should consistently refer to "blocks" to avoid confusion with the Session report.

57-66: parseTokenLimit still accepts 0 / negative numbers — divide-by-zero risk
A prior review already flagged this, but the implementation was not updated.
0 (or <0) propagates to % calculations and JSON projection (projection.totalTokens / limit) causing Infinity, NaN, or runtime ZeroDivisionError equivalents.
- const limit = Number.parseInt(value, 10);
- return Number.isNaN(limit) ? undefined : limit;
+ const limit = Number.parseInt(value, 10);
+ if (Number.isNaN(limit) || limit <= 0) {
+   return undefined; // invalid
+ }
+ return limit;
Please also add a unit test covering "0", "-1", and "max" paths.

src/data-loader.ts (1)
897-911: Reuse filterByDateRange() instead of open-coded string compare
The bespoke date check duplicates the earlier filterByDateRange helper but is slightly different (empty-string handling, replace(/-/g,'') etc.). Divergent logic risks subtle regressions.
- const filtered = (options?.since ... )
-   ? blocks.filter(/* manual compare */)
-   : blocks;
+ const filtered = filterByDateRange(
+   blocks,
+   b => b.startTime.toISOString(),

This keeps behaviour consistent across all loaders and removes ~15 lines.

active, recent, and especially tokenLimit flags plus parseTokenLimit() logic have been duplicated once already (see previous review). Move them into sharedCommandConfig or a tiny blocks-args.ts to avoid repeating validation & help-text in future commands.

Summary
This PR implements a new blocks command to analyze Claude Code usage in 5-hour billing windows as requested in #23.
Features

5-Hour Block Tracking: Groups usage into Claude's 5-hour session windows that start with first message
Active Block Monitoring: Shows time elapsed/remaining and burn rate for current sessions
Token Limit Support: Set limits with -t <number> or use -t max to automatically use highest previous block
Usage Projections: Projects total usage if current burn rate continues for the full 5 hours
Recent Filter: --recent flag shows only last 3 days of blocks
Detailed Active View: --active flag shows detailed view of current active block

Implementation Details

Core logic in src/utils/five-hour-blocks.ts handles block detection and calculations
New CLI command in src/commands/blocks.ts with table and JSON output formats
Integrated with existing data loader infrastructure
Added comprehensive documentation to README

Example Output

│                                                        │ Status      │                         │        │        │         │
├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┼─────────────┼─────────────────────────┼────────┼────────┼─────────┤
│ 6/16/2025, 6:21:16 PM (1h 25m elapsed, 3h 35m remain) │ ACTIVE      │ claude-opus-4-20250514  │ 25,979 │ 41.8%  │ $74.54  │
├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┼─────────────┼─────────────────────────┼────────┼────────┼─────────┤

├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┼─────────────┼─────────────────────────┼────────┼────────┼─────────┤
│                       (assuming current burn rate)    │ PROJECTED   │                         │ 91,443 │ 147.3% │ $262.09 │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┴─────────────┴─────────────────────────┴────────┴────────┴─────────┘

Testing

All existing tests pass
TypeScript compilation successful
Manual testing with various scenarios including active blocks, token limits, and edge cases

Fixes #23

Enhanced output options with JSON formatting and customizable display modes.


Documentation

Updated the README with a comprehensive section on the new 5-hour blocks report, including usage examples and feature descriptions.

Summary
This PR implements a new blocks command to analyze Claude Code usage in 5-hour billing windows as requested in #23.
Features

5-Hour Block Tracking: Groups usage into Claude's 5-hour session windows that start with first message
Active Block Monitoring: Shows time elapsed/remaining and burn rate for current sessions
Token Limit Support: Set limits with -t <number> or use -t max to automatically use highest previous block
Usage Projections: Projects total usage if current burn rate continues for the full 5 hours
Recent Filter: --recent flag shows only last 3 days of blocks
Detailed Active View: --active flag shows detailed view of current active block

Implementation Details

Core logic in src/utils/five-hour-blocks.ts handles block detection and calculations
New CLI command in src/commands/blocks.ts with table and JSON output formats
Integrated with existing data loader infrastructure
Added comprehensive documentation to README

All existing tests pass

70-72: Remove unreachable null-check on lastEntry.
currentBlockEntries always contains at least one element once we’re inside the else branch (we push the first entry when the block is opened).
The guard adds noise and can be safely deleted.
-			const lastEntry = currentBlockEntries.at(-1);
-			if (lastEntry == null) {
-				continue;

+			const lastEntry = currentBlockEntries.at(-1); // never null



🧹 Nitpick comments (2)

src/utils/five-hour-blocks.ts (2)
113-114: isActive may become stale shortly after computation.
now is captured once at the start of identifyFiveHourBlocks and passed to every block.
If the caller re-uses the resulting blocks for longer-running CLI output or caching, a block that was active may appear inactive minutes later (and vice-versa).
Consider computing isActive lazily (getter) or recalculating with the real-time clock when the value is consumed.

160-162: Gap block endTime stretches beyond 5 h window.
While the comment on endTime now acknowledges that gap blocks use nextActivityTime, consumers still need to branch on isGap to reason about block length.
A cleaner design is a discriminated union:
type NormalBlock = { isGap?: false; endTime: Date /* start + 5h */; ... }
type GapBlock    = { isGap: true;  gapEndTime: Date; endTime?: never; ... }
This enforces invariants at compile-time and removes implicit contracts from JSDoc.
